name: Ogalla

attributes.attribute: held sacred for its fresh and salt water
converted the princesses at the spring

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Ogalla is an Irish mythological site. The Celts held fresh and salt water in reverence, and placed many tales at or by water. Streams and wells, clear water rising from the ground, had a central place in Irish tradition. One such tale tells of two Connacht princesses, Eithne and Fedelm. They came to wash in the holy spring at Ogalla, near the great capital of Cruachan. There they met white-robed men, Druid-like in their eyes. The men were not Druids. The men were Saint Patrick and his followers. The princesses put questions to Patrick about his god. Was it in earth, sky, or sea? Did he have fine daughters, sons fair? Patrick answered that the one god was all they wished (avoiding the daughters). The princesses converted, then chose to die at once of baptism rather than remain in the world of sin. The close is as un-Celtic as the girls' questions were pagan.

okr.objective: Ogalla is an Irish site where two princesses met Saint Patrick.
key_results: The Celts held fresh and salt water sacred.
Eithne and Fedelm were princesses of Connacht.
They met Saint Patrick and his followers at the spring.
Both chose to die at baptism rather than live in sin.
